title: Repairing a Rotted Cast-Iron Toilet Flange with a Retrofit Gasket and Spacer System

locations.name: Underneath the toilet (floor area)
locations.basis: Discussion of the wax seal location and leak path beneath the toilet; remodel context implies floor area under the toilet.

locations.name: In the truck (demonstration setting)
locations.basis: Host says 'down in the truck' to show a cutaway; not confirmed as the filming location.

summary: This Old House’s tutorial walks through diagnosing a leak tied to a failed wax seal and a rotted cast-iron closet flange after a bathroom remodel. The host explains toilet anatomy (trapway, siphon jet, and flange), identifies a downstroom stoppage as the likely leak cause, then shuts off water and removes the toilet. A remodel revealed the old cast-iron flange was missing or severely degraded, prompting a retrofit approach: replace with a gasket-style flange adapter designed for cast-iron pipe, using spacers to set the correct height, and switching from a traditional wax seal to a flexible gasket. The video covers removing corroded bolts with a mini-hacksaw, reassembling with new closet bolts and washers, and confirming a leak-free connection after restoring water supply.
topics: Remodel height changes (tile floor vs flange height)
Gasket-based retrofit flange with Allen screws

sections.title: Symptom identification
sections.description: The scene opens with the toilet clogging, followed by water dripping on the ceiling beneath, prompting concern that a downstream issue or a seal failure could be causing the leak.

sections.title: Toilet anatomy (cutaway) and functions
sections.description: A cutaway illustration demonstrates how a siphon-jet toilet operates, the role of the trapway, and how the closet flange attaches the bowl to the plumbing, laying groundwork for diagnosing the leak path.

sections.title: Likely cause of leak: downstream stoppage and wax seal
sections.description: The presenter reasons the stoppage occurred below the bowl, pushing pressure backward and causing wax-seal leaks visible in the ceiling, rather than a blockage in the trap itself.

sections.title: Shutoff and drain preparation
sections.description: Water is shut off at the valve, the tank is drained with the float adjusted, and a sponge is used to remove remaining water so the toilet can be removed safely.

sections.title: Toilet removal and initial inspections
sections.description: The toilet is lifted off the flange after disconnecting the bolts; a crack in the toilet is noted and the bolts prove to be rusted, complicating removal.

sections.title: Reveal of remodel and flange condition
sections.description: Removal reveals remodel work that raised the tile floor, showing the old cast-iron flange lower than the finished floor and the subfloor exposure surrounding it.

sections.title: Flange alternatives considered
sections.description: Discussion of historical methods (lead-and-hemp packing) and the difficulty of fitting a modern flange to the existing pipe due to size, prompting consideration of retrofit options.

sections.title: Install retrofit gasket flange and height setting
sections.description: A gasket-based retrofit flange with four Allen screws is chosen to seal the connection to the cast-iron pipe; spacers are added to position the flange at the correct height and align the bolt keyway.

sections.title: Final assembly and testing
sections.description: The toilet is reassembled with proper bolts and a flexible gasket, water is turned back on, and a leak-free connection is confirmed after testing.
